title: Average and Instantaneous Speed and Velocity
learning_objective: Formulate average velocity as net displacement over total time, instantaneous velocity as the time derivative of position, and understand the difference between average speed and average velocity magnitude.
intuition: When driving a car, your trip may take 2 hours to cover a 100 km curved highway, giving an average speed of 50 km/h. At any split second during the drive, glancing at the speedometer displays your instantaneous speed (e.g. 70 km/h), while the direction the front of your car points gives the direction of your instantaneous velocity vector.
formal_definition: The average velocity over a finite time interval $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$ is $\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\vec{r}}{\Delta t} = \frac{\vec{r}(t_2) - \vec{r}(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}$. The instantaneous velocity $\vec{v}(t)$ is the derivative of position with respect to time: $\vec{v}(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta\vec{r}}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$. Instantaneous speed $v(t) = |\vec{v}(t)| = \frac{ds}{dt}$ is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity, whereas average speed is total distance divided by total time: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{s_{\text{total}}}{t_{\text{total}}}$.
explanation:
Velocity is the fundamental vector kinematic quantity characterizing rate of change of position.

### 1. Direction of Instantaneous Velocity
The instantaneous velocity vector $\vec{v}(t)$ is always tangent to the particle's spatial path at every point, pointing in the direction of motion. In Cartesian coordinates, $\vec{v} = v_x\hat{i} + v_y\hat{j} + v_z\hat{k} = \frac{dx}{dt}\hat{i} + \frac{dy}{dt}\hat{j} + \frac{dz}{dt}\hat{k}$.

### 2. Average Velocity vs Average Speed
While $|\vec{v}(t)| = v(t)$ is true at every instant, $|\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}| \le v_{\text{avg}}$ over any finite interval because $|\Delta\vec{r}| \le s_{\text{total}}$. For closed trajectories (such as one complete lap on a circular track), the net displacement is zero, yielding $\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \vec{0}$, while the average speed is strictly positive: $v_{\text{avg}} = 2\pi R / T > 0$.

### 3. Calculus Perspective
Feynman emphasized in Lecture 8 that defining velocity as $dx/dt$ requires taking a limit where both $\Delta x$ and $\Delta t$ shrink to zero, yet their ratio approaches a well-defined physical rate.
assumptions: Position function $\vec{r}(t)$ is continuous and differentiable over the time domain.
boundary_conditions: If $\vec{v}$ is constant, average velocity equals instantaneous velocity for any interval.
Average speed is never smaller than the magnitude of average velocity.
source_references: Concepts of Physics Vol 1 by H.C. Verma (Chapter 3, pp. 44-47)
The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. 1 (Lecture 8: Motion, pp. 81-85)
